member.name: T:GameLauncher.Desktop.Models.CatalogAlias
member.summary: Maps one fingerprint onto a catalog entry.

remarks.para: A single title legitimately produces several fingerprints. A re-release changes the product name; a game shipped with a separate launcher has one fingerprint for the launcher and another for the game itself; two storefronts ship builds with different company strings. Modelling that as many aliases to one entry means those are recognised as the same title without any of them being declared "wrong".

member.name: T:GameLauncher.Desktop.Models.CatalogEntry
member.summary: The shared identity of a game title, as opposed to one person's installation of it.

remarks.para: This is the anchor every cross-user feature hangs off. Achievements, stats and — in future — presence and cloud sync all reference rather than a local Game.Id, because a local identifier means nothing to anybody else: two people who own the same game have different rows, different integer keys and different Game.GlobalKey values.

An entry begins life , with an id minted locally and prefixed local:, so the launcher is fully functional offline and without a relay configured. On first contact with a relay the entry is promoted: the relay either recognises the and returns the existing catalog id, or assigns a new one. Promotion rewrites the primary key, and every reference follows automatically through ON UPDATE CASCADE.

member.summary: Reconnect schedule for the relay connection: exponential backoff with jitter, capped, and never giving up.

remarks.para: Never returning is deliberate. member.summary: Default , built on the Win32 icon APIs.

remarks.para: Two extraction paths are attempted in order. PrivateExtractIcons is tried first because it accepts an explicit size and can return the 256-pixel image modern executables embed; ExtractIconEx is the fallback and returns the system large icon, which is 32 pixels on a standard-DPI display. The order matters for how the library looks: a 32-pixel icon stretched across a 150x225 cover tile is visibly blurred, whereas the 256-pixel image is sharp.
Every handle obtained from either API is released with DestroyIcon. Icon handles are a finite per-session GDI resource, and a folder scan can extract hundreds in a few seconds.
